Long before kings, cities or farms, the land we call India was a wild world of forests, rivers and grasslands.
So who were the very first humans to walk here? And how did they get here?
Our story begins far away, in Africa.
That is where the human family first evolved. And around two million years ago, early humans called Homo erectus began to walk out of Africa.
They spread across Asia, and some of them reached the Indian subcontinent.
How do we know? Because they left behind their tools.
In 1863, a British geologist named Robert Bruce Foote picked up a stone hand axe at Pallavaram, near Chennai.
It was the first Old Stone Age tool ever identified in India.
Since then, thousands of such tools have been found across the subcontinent.
At Attirampakkam in Tamil Nadu, scientists dated stone tools to about one and a half million years ago.
That makes them some of the oldest tools of their kind found anywhere outside Africa.
In Karnataka, the Hunsgi and Isampur valleys hold entire workshops, where early humans shaped stone, again and again.
Historians call this period the Palaeolithic, or the Old Stone Age.
It is divided into three stages.
In the Lower Palaeolithic, people made large hand axes and cleavers.
In the Middle Palaeolithic, they made smaller, sharper tools from flakes of stone.
And in the Upper Palaeolithic, they made thin blades, tools of bone, and their very first art.
But what did these people look like?
In 1982, at Hathnora in the Narmada valley, geologist Arun Sonakia found part of an ancient human skull.
Known as Narmada Man, it is one of the very few early human fossils ever found in India. Its exact age is still debated.
Then, around seventy-four thousand years ago, disaster struck.
A super-volcano called Toba erupted in Sumatra. It was one of the largest eruptions in the last two million years.
Its ash fell across India. At Jwalapuram in Andhra Pradesh, archaeologists found stone tools both below and above this ash.
Did humans survive the blast? Scientists are still debating.
What we do know is that modern humans, people like us, reached India by around fifty to seventy thousand years ago. Some researchers think even earlier.
They lived as hunter-gatherers, moving with the seasons, following animals and water.
They hunted deer and wild cattle, gathered fruits, roots and honey, and sheltered in caves and rock shelters.
Like early humans everywhere, they used fire, for warmth, for light, and for cooking.
At Patne in Maharashtra, archaeologists found pieces of ostrich eggshell, carefully engraved, and made into beads.
These people were not just survivors. They were thinkers, and artists.
And their greatest masterpieces were still to come.
